text: I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created. By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps. The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes. But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out. It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

I've been a Principal Engineer for a while, so this is how I've worked for a while. Sometimes when you're a PE, you either design something and then junior engineers implement the details, or you're dropped into a project that was already designed and built by more junior engineers, and you have to quickly understand the design an as many details as you can. With AI, everyone now gets to act like a PE. Your job is to design, the AI builds like the junior engineers. Then you review their work. You may never understand the details, and that's ok, as long as you know the main ideas and where to ask for the details (in this case the LLM instead of a human).

Testing. Lots and lots of testing. I usually interactively test with the LLM. Now that I'm spending less time, coding, I get to spend more time, testing. In my experience, I test more, with an LLM, than I did, with my own code. I don't find coding errors, but I do find implementation errors. On another note: I ran an LLM on a bunch of really mature code that I wrote, and could swear was "perfect," and it found a number of issues. Nobody's perfect. Trust; but verify .

I’m slowly coming around to the idea that if it works, I’m good with that. I never used to personally check all my colleagues work, either, I just trusted that they’d done a good job. That’s not to say I blindly trust an LLM - my project is an autovectorising compiler. I have it write a bazillion tests, and I have real, non-trivial programs that it compiled. I have it run a ‘gate’ before releases that takes literally hours on 5 different architectures. To say this code is tested is … masterful understatement. I think what helps is a long planning session, going into details, working out corner cases, designing test-cases, you know work and effort. Once that’s done it’s easier to let it work through the night and do a major production feature. I still review the code, but hand on heart I couldn’t say I’d reviewed everything , sometimes I miss something in a complicated check-in. I try to keep checkins small and contained, but sometimes that’s not easy to manage alongside the “don’t break stuff” rule as well. So it comes down to: I’ve been working on this for 6 months or so, and so far this has worked out for me. You know, kind of like getting used to a colleague’s idiosyncrasies over a period of time. I will say that in my experience the code quality is fairly high. Maybe that’s down to the effort put in ahead of time in the planning stages, I don’t know, but I don’t seem to suffer from the ‘slop’ that people complain of. YMMV.

The closer the code gets to the user's eyeballs the less I care about anything specific. HTML/JS/CSS is basically entirely vibe coded. I won't even try to reorg the 4000 line ui.js file. I can just redo the whole thing from a new prompt in a few minutes. For things like the SQL schema I am still doing things entirely by hand. The consequences of getting this part wrong tend to be far more catastrophic than something in the UI layer.

These threads kind of rule. Lots of different answers! For my part: I've put some of my tooling energy into code comprehension tools. You can get remarkably far quickly by just replacing the Github PR viewer! I started with a (native SwiftUI) read-only front end for tree-sitter and SCIP (the code-indexing standard). Then: as I reviewed PRs, I tried to catch myself doing annoying repetitive things and just building out additional features, like "show me all the knowable call chains for this function", or "show me every implementation of this trait". You can get a fair ways just by thinking of things to hide in a PR viewer, just to clear space for the things you need to comprehend.

It's not too dissimilar to life as a Principal level engineer pre-AI. You technically oversee the work of many engineers on their own systems, but you couldn't possibly review all the code yourself. You appreciate that human code review reduces, but does not eliminate, the number and severity of bugs shipped to production. You don't have the low-level details in your head, just the high-level ones. You design how all these engineers interact with each other, without stepping on any toes. Time will tell whether we were right to move from a system where we trusted humans to understand the low-level system, to one where we trust fancy calculators. But so far, it's working.

I lost my ability to fully explain the systems I work on around the time I transitioned from next-edit-prediction AI running in my IDE (early Copilot) and working primarily via Codex/Claude CLI's. The further away I got from the implementation details, the fuzzier the semantics became. To the point that now I could not in good faith say I understand the system I have built from the ground-up and worked on the last ~4-5 years. The solution to this, in my mind, is not to revert back to reviewing implementation details. The economics of that from a business/productivity perspective don't play out well. The only viable solution in my mind is adapting code/languages themselves to the shift by making programs formally verifiable. That way you can be sure that the code "does what it says on the tin", and provably so. I feel so strongly about this I've written on it: https://gavinray97.github.io/blog/design-by-contract-and-eff... (https://gavinray97.github.io/blog/design-by-contract-and-effects-for-llms)

I can think of so many times this has happened before. People getting used to MVC, Dependency Injection, ORMs. Sometimes the code is so large you only work on a part of it, so you have to get used to a lot of not knowing. So how do we build confidence anyhow when we can't know everything? I think first, standard checks - does it compile? What do static analysis tools say - code quality, passes SAST analysis? Linters? Style checkers? Do the tests run? I'm not comfortable with the tests I write let alone the AI.. by adding fault injection (fuzzing, chaos), and mutation testing, I have a better degree of confidence in the tests and code. Spend even more time getting to know the product instead. Maybe I don't know the code as well as I used to, but I know the product backwards and forwards. That helps me have some new confidence that I didn't really have before. Knowing the greater whole.
I'm miles away from all of this as a non-user of AI and it seems like a mania to me.

Tests, observability metrics/alerts, and backups. Worst case, I can rollback everything to a point-in-time where the system is stable. You have to design your process for writing code to handle more code than you could ever read. To do this you also have to accept that you will not be able to hand manage all of your agents and all of your projects. The key thing is to figure out how to manage your time better and spend your efforts unblocking your agents. What I did was build my own process for this: https://github.com/mhalstrom/maximizepm (https://github.com/mhalstrom/maximizepm) The main take away is: 1. You need an agent to manage your agents that you mainly interact with. 2. You need a durable way to manage tasks and the dependencies between them. 3. You need agents with multiple roles ie manage, build, review etc 4. You need to manage yourself across projects so any system you build needs to take that into account

If you work at Meta you should ask at Meta. For my own projects I’ve limited my exposure points by picking which projects and what scope I ship. I have to iOS apps in the App Store and I simply removed high exposure surfaces - right now neither use accounts because I don’t want to manage account systems, and Apple prefers it anyway. I downrisked my projects from what I could ship and I’m perfectly happy with my production projects. Most of my other AI written projects are internal apps and systems. I have another project going public soon where I ship the output of LLM written code, without running the code in any user accessible area. And tests, of course. In time things will mature, tooling will be better, and we’ll have a different risk quotient.

The time that I would have spent typing in the code is now time I use to test the code. I really like to poke at things and ensure that my understanding and reality match. I agree with the advice to design your system before implementing it. It is pretty easy to iterate on a design with your favorite coding assistant, and this is your chance to be ultra-picky and make sure you get exactly what you want. This was always where the "software engineering" was done, but in practice it's easy to have a vague idea and refine your (internal) list of requirements / tradeoffs as you type in the code. I find it harder to do that when the LLM is generating the code, just because one turn can change so much. Keeping it under control requires discipline, just like before LLMs were a thing. You set a bunch of engineers loose on your codebase with no vision or supervision, you get spaghetti. You just get a little bit more control now. Agents don't feel shitty for the rest of the day when you tell them to do it some other way, so you are free to review as critically as you want without hurting anyone's feelings. I think it's a good thing.

1) Need to triple down on infrastructure (safeguards, tests, sandboxes, etc.). 2) Ask agents to do more than just code. They need to fully demonstrate and prove that their PRs are rock solid. Ask for screenshots, videos, code reviews, detailed architecture diagrams, etc. It would be an insane amount of work for humans, but AI can do it easily for each PR. Merging any PR from an agent should be a no-brainer if there's real proof that the feature is built correctly and working. If there's still doubt, then the agent needs to do a better job of proving that the feature is built correctly, doesn't introduce regressions, etc.

"Great leaders hire smart people and step aside so those experts can guide and solve problems instead of being micromanaged" - Ask questions, clarify and ask "Do you have any questions". - Build systems for robustness, like you would build when delegating to human engineers. Tests are just an important but small part of it. (Take ownership) - Lead with examples (not just skills.md or what-i-want.md). It cannot understand your abstractions. - Peer reviews (Across agents or across models) - Clear division of responsibilities (Context engineering - Agents/SubAgents)

The traditional answer is the same for engineers going into engineering management because managing a team and managing a set of agents is highly similar, only managing agents is far easier. One only ever has the illusion of control, and so you have to set your mind to containing the worst possible outcomes and looking at the net efficiency and efficacy of the team with the understanding that they will, on average, never be perfect.

This is as much a top-down issue (managers incentivising AI use and high velocity) as much as it is a bottom-up issue (devs knocking out issues faster than they can review) It's a problem that requires a united approach from both sides. A need to pace oneself, as it were.

* Focus on the data models. Design them carefully. * Review any code that modify the data (when possible, avoid migrations that can't be rolled back) * Staging/PR deployments/feature flags * Observability * End-to-end black box integration tests for the main features (unit tests are mostly useless)

I'm surprised by a lot of the commenters here. People that are saying just wait for all these codebases to crumble for us to be needed again refuse to acknowledge the reality of what is happening around us. If that is your take, I advise you to become really, really good at programming and work somewhere in the realm of critical infrastructure or financial institutions where presumably agent written code will be last to permeate. I do get the sentiment but the conclusion doesn't make sense to me. We have been solving problems as engineers at different layers of abstraction for a long time. Pre-AI, I used frameworks that abstracted lower level concepts away which made it faster to develop the solutions that mattered (aka solving problems for the end user). I could, given enough time, write the underlying database adapter to convert my business logic form into a database query and back out but I didn't need to because someone else abstracted that part away. Did I know how well that adapter was written? No. Were there bugs in it? Occasionally you run into a limitation or bug the author hadn't considered that required a patch or fix. Going a step deeper, the programming language itself is an abstraction that compiles into machine code or bytecode. Do I understand machine code or kernels? Definitely not. Some programmers do, especially if you have a compsci background, but I'd wager the number has been decreasing over the years. The point is, now agents are writing code and they are now pretty damn good at it. Better than the "average" programmer out there. Now we get to "program" in natural language by telling the agents what we want and they get to worry about nailing the syntax and all those details while we focus on the higher level decision and direction of what's happening. If your agent written code is sloppy and terrible, that's a skill issue not an agents write bad code issue. You need to setup the systems that result in code to your standards with the checks and balances to test and QA appropriately before it hits production. Complaining about the state of things while sitting back with your arms crossed refusing to adapt to this bold new world is a risky strategy. People saying just don't use AI and do your job as normal are also going to have a difficult time. The devs that can leverage AI effectively and get a lot done will out leverage you to the point where it doesn't make economical sense to keep paying you to not use AI (unless you are in one of those super critical fields I mentioned earlier and even then I'm not sure those are safe). Isn't it more fun to embrace this new technology and figure out how to use it effectively vs complaining and refusing to acknowledge it? Help shape the future instead.

Build tools to help you understand. Build metrics that are proxies for the things you'd care about. Add constraints to the agent's work related to performance, error monitoring, language and architecture choices, review bots (that you tune and eventually, trust). If you don't have good ideas for tools, ask Fable what the best coders and industry experts would look at to establish trust, then feed that into models to build it. Don't sleep on how useful something like a (data-backed) claude artifact can be - i setup one today to track dependency and known vulnerabilties with a burndown chart and (agent) run log, one prompt, it was usable 5 minutes later. A colleague of mine did the same, but as a datadog notebook that also wires in relevant API metrics depending on what code has gone out in the last week, and suggests new longer term metrics to monitor as a result. Etc etc. its a crazy world but this has helped me cope so far.

Maybe a bit unorthodox but I have it plant 1-3 bugs into the code it writes (depending on the size of the MR I'm working on); they range from simple one-off issues to something more structural. It then gives me a hint on the area or a typical code flow that would hit the bug - whichever gives me less info. I can obviously ask for more hints as I read along. Obviously all honour-code based since I could just ask it to fix the bugs itself. I think this is something that can't be fixed systemically - either you're going to bother reading and thinking through the code or not. Other than that I guess reading the tests - to make sure they fail without the code / fix, to make sure the setup makes sense etc.

A major part of my job (and this was true before the "AI boom") is saying no. No we can't call the CRM from our client side using a static bearer token even though their docs say we can. No we can't simply switch to Postgres even though it supports 99% of the same SQL we currently use. No we can't simply block usernames which are "clearly" profane. But if we can chat about it, then we can see what the REAL problem is, and then we can come up with a fitting and simple solution. The problem is that I have an AI colleague who is way more energetic and willing than I am. They love to talk, they seem to ramble on endlessly about any subject. And its the kind of solution oriented talk my PM loves to hear. And indeed my <insert senior role here> talks to them (or really, lets them talk), and draws up a comprehensive and confident plan to do X. I pick up the plan and discover problems with X, let alone the plan to do it. I feel nervous about raising issues with X or going through the plan again though, because my other human colleagues are already speeding through the work for Y and Z that my AI colleague is aiding with. And so maybe I'll raise my biggest concerns with X and not sweat the small stuff. Maybe next time I won't raise my neck at all, noting the gleaming axe sitting in the corner.

Test driven development and the testing pyramid. If the agent has written tests and crucially - witnessed them fail before starting the work to make them pass - you have a lot of confidence. Review of your own work's easier too - test and production code tend to mirror each other, giving you a much more complete picture. Confused by the production code? Go read its tests for a bit, then come back. It's also easier to understand the change if you were there for the build, watching the transcript, checking in every so often. Doesn't have to be your primary task - leave it on a second monitor, it'll catch your eye naturally. And finally, on top of test-driven development, have the agent first (before the first test driven development cycle) build out an end-to-end test covering the work it'll do. Once that test is green (test driven word for "is passing") you're done with your work and can clean up at will. Play with it before shipping, get it real nice. It's never been easier to clean the tech debt up and make the UI perfect . Eventually you'll be ready to package it up into a PR! Now's you can leverage agents and get creative. Make your colleagues froth to review your work. Consider making a Loom video to walk them through it. Consider reworking it into a commit series; it only takes a few second for your agent and you can tell a story for humans. Maybe you want to sequence it according to your struggles; maybe it's better to show the different layers emerge with each commit - it's up to you. Consider also that your agent can easily do one-off visualizations of the change for your colleagues if you think it'll help them, and you can attach those too - mermaid charts or even whimsical AI generated images. All this is because motivation is driven entirely by other humans' motivation and you want them frothing with excitement every time you drop a review. Make it fun, it takes seconds and gets your stuff merged fast while making your teammates smile. This is a brand new job and we will work out how to do it together :)

I've been spending a lot of time iterating on feature implementation plans with Claude (at work) and GPT (for personal projects). I then make sure they write a lot of tests and that if functionality is changed or added/removed then tests are updated alongside. Generally I try to review changes myself and ask it to explain the changes. It's not perfect but I feel like the planning step being iterative isn't all too different from my old research -> think about implementation -> implement loop. At that point, reviewing any code changes goes hand in hand with how I coded before LLMs. The major difference is I usually have it make any changes for things I don't like.

I'm currently working on a combined Aero sim/CAD/CAM software for designing, simulating, and performing DFM optimization specifically for Group 1 to 3 winged UAVs. What I do is ask Opus/Gemini to explain the parts I don't understand. And I do some of my own research to verify accuracy of the explanations. In addition: * Every new feature has a Feature Design document which I review, modify, and approve. And a corresponding Implementation Plan which I also review and approve. * Every fix has a RCA document and fix Implementation Doc which I review, modify, and approve. * There's a global high level Architecture and Design document with additional sub component design documents which are always kept in synch after a new feature or bug fix is done. Synching it is always a step in the Implementation plan. This does adds some overhead but it allows me to have have check point gates. This has often allowed me to catch misunderstandings and align properly before any code gets edited by the AI agent. Having the above docs also helps when it comes to referencing them as context to properly ground new features or bug fixes.

Peter Naur in 1985 wrote that programming is the act of building a working theory of the system in our minds, and this often takes form as tacit knowledge in the head of programmers. Even if you handed the complete codebase and perfect documentation to a completely new team, they would often need to go back to the old team and ask questions. And before agents, we often built this working theory of the system by writing the code by hand. It helps us figure out the "grain" of the codebase so we have a better idea of how to extend it. So what happens when agents are writing the code? The main avenue with which we built the working theory of the system in our mind is now taken away, and we're left feeling like our understanding of the system is blinded. I ended up more or less changing my entire workflow. Four main principles: 1. Interrogation/interview-based design and specification 2. Make the decisions that matter and leave the rest to the agent. 3. Use agent to generate explainers, quizzes, and simulations. 4. Use verifiers and guardrails in the coding loop. Interview-based design and spec When I tell the agent what I want to build or extend, there's naturally ambiguity. But the agent knows what is ambiguous to it, so it can ask me. /grill-me is one way to do this. You'd think this would be commonplace now, but it's actually not. Some people are still wondering why they're getting bad results. It's because they're not resolving the ambiguity. Making the decisions that matter Not every decision matters in a product. Agents are fast at writing code and pretty good at some of the nitty gritty details, so I let it make those decisions. Also, if a particular subsystem is commonplace and undifferentiating, such as login, then I also let it make architectural decisions for that subsystem. For decisions that are product differentiators, where that differentiation is supported by technology, I make decisions on the stack, the architecture, and the approach. This is the design phase. Because agents tend to make the mainstream decisions, they almost always take a midwit approach which doesn't leverage the technology in a way that makes a difference for the customer. Some try to build this understanding from code reviews. I personally don't think it's the way to go, because it's not motivating. I find that I'm more motivated to learn how the system works today, because I want to change how it works tomorrow--and it sticks in my head better too (no different than pre-agents). Generating explainers, quizzes, and simulations As I'm doing design for an improvement and I don't know how a part of the system works, I can ask questions of the agent in chat. If I still don't get it, I can ask for diagrams (either ASCII or mermaid). But if it's an entire subsystem, I have a skill in which I can ask for visual and interactive explainers. It'll generate a markdown page (or html) that has these interactive components that help demonstrate a concept. To help make the concept stick, there are quizzes after each section and at the end. With the computational simulations, I generate a throwaway tool in which I can explore the state space. This doesn't happen as often, as I try to keep state spaces small, and for those explainers tend to work well. With the design simulations, a same-model agent and a cross-model agent and I will talk about an explainer, and we'll name things that we understand or notice about the design and the intended direction we want to extend it. Then, we'll use subagents to generate options and then discuss the pros and cons. I find this is a good way for me to understand the dead-ends of a design. Using Verifiers and Guardrails I define guardrails as mechanistic checks that doesn't change with the feature. such as linters, typecheckers, and pre-commit hooks are all guardrails. Verifiers are mechanistic checks that will be different with each feature, such as unit/integration tests. For more complicated states or concurrent parts, I'll ask the agent to use formal methods to write a proof. Then use the proof to generate a trace (a series of steps that demonstrate a happy or unhappy path). Then I run that trace in unit tests (kinda like property-based testing--so I guess this can be called trace-based testing), and the code has to adhere to the trace. I also wrote a design verifier, where the requirements in the spec can be converted into a series of mechanically checkable rules. Then during testing, the verifier fires up the headless browser and uses the DOM measurements of the page to see if it matches up to the rules. This was completely impractical before agents. All of this so a) I can be sure that the agent is doing what it's supposed to with the decisions that it's making b) I can be out of the coding loop, so that I'm not up at 2am begging, "you fixed this, but you broke that. pls fix." The agent can check for itself. --- If any of this sounds helpful, lemme know. Anyone who trusts the output of LLMs uncritically, even after the impressive level models and harnesses have gotten to, is borrowing against their future. Models and harnesses have gotten really good, but they still are hard-capped by the operators that use them. The sycophancy of models is perhaps their greatest weakness, as when a user who might be experienced in one area attempts to use AI to build within an area they are less familiar with, the model does not take a step back and examine the "why" of what is being built from an architectural standpoint, it simply performs the expected task in a direct manner, ultimately creating sloppy work that may be easy to ship but difficult to maintain. A good example of this was a recent interaction I had with a Dev who was very familiar with how to develop embedded and system level applications. He and every other dev are being asked for increasingly more due to AI, and he had to bring something he had built as a single-user desktop application into a distributed cloud environment. He ended up rsyncing a copy of his working directories including multiple credentials and sensitive internal project documents to a virtual machine binding it to a public ip address. Thankfully our tooling detected this before he could get any farther but it illustrates how the AI model isn't doing any real thinking or engineering at the end of the day. Unless the operator knew to instruct the model about proper cloud architecture and understood best practices around deployment of public systems, the model simply did what it was being told to do by a user who didn't know any better. Another example of this is the sheer amount of unsophisticated users we've been detecting using Javascript injection into their web browser sessions as a form of automation for web services they may use. These users would never know to ask how to request an API token which may allow them to accomplish things in a much easier and approved way, and instead are relying on the frailest possible automations that expose them to risks of credential exposure. We've got to be careful with how we engineer things with AI models. Just because we've made boilerplate easier to generate doesn't mean that we can avoid the actual engineering of what we do. And I can't help but think that firms which are fully committed to AI code generation, won't just be introducing an avalanche of slop into their product which will explode the costs of maintenance over time.

In my experience you're just replicating the problem. Slop code doesn't stop being slop code when you add in slop tests to account for the sloppiness. If you generate code at a certain velocity, you eventually get to a point where you generate tests the same way you generate code. The model does its best effort in creating tests, but you'll inevitably get to a point in your work where the tests themselves are faulty and unreliable, the same sloppiness you were trying to control for. There have been multiple times where my software dev team has gone back to prior implemented tests they had the model generate and found that after some time eventually the model got frustrated with the test no longer passing eventually modifying it to fit current needs around a feature push. You can probably anticipate how we came to discover this, as it ended up introducing a regression around multiple edge cases which the test was meant to control for. The only answer is to inject actual engineering into the process as much as possible without giving it all up to the models to generate more slop in response to slop. tests are a great answer, but only if you treat them with serious intentionality.
